question: The two types of weather satellite orbit are:

options.text: Polar orbiting and geostationary
Low equatorial and high polar
Sun-synchronous and lunar-synchronous only
Equatorial orbiting and lunar

explanation: Polar orbiters pass low over the poles giving detailed images; geostationary satellites stay over one point on the Equator giving a continuous view.

question: A geostationary weather satellite orbits:

options.text: Over the poles at about 850 km, taking about 100 minutes per orbit
Over the poles at about 36 000 km, taking 24 hours per orbit
Over the Equator at about 850 km, taking about 100 minutes per orbit
Over the Equator at about 36 000 km, taking 24 hours per orbit

explanation: Matching the Earth's rotation keeps it fixed relative to the ground, so it can image the same area continuously.

question: The main advantage of a geostationary satellite over a polar orbiter is:

options.text: Much higher picture definition than any polar orbiter
A continuous view of the same area, for time-lapse sequences
The ability to see through cloud to the surface below
Better coverage of the polar regions than any other orbit

explanation: Its great height means lower resolution and distortion near the poles, but the continuous coverage is far more valuable for tracking weather.

question: Images from geostationary satellites become distorted:

options.text: Only at night, when the sensors cool
Over the Equator, directly below the satellite, where it is closest
Towards the poles, which it views at a very low angle
Only over the oceans, which have no features

explanation: Being above the Equator, the satellite sees high latitudes obliquely. Computer processing can partly correct this.

question: A geostationary satellite such as Meteosat over the Greenwich meridian covers roughly:

options.text: About one third of the Earth's surface, from about 70°W to 70°E
Only the polar regions, where it is most needed
The whole globe, including both poles, every few minutes, day and night
Only Europe and the North Atlantic

explanation: Several geostationary satellites spaced around the Equator are needed for near-global coverage outside the polar regions.

question: A polar-orbiting weather satellite typically:

options.text: Stays permanently above the North Pole, viewing the hemisphere
Orbits at about 36 000 km, taking 24 hours, remaining over one fixed point
Orbits only over the Equator, at about 850 km
Orbits at about 850 km, taking about 100 minutes, scanning a wide strip

explanation: Low altitude gives good detail, and the Earth rotating beneath it brings each successive pass further west.

question: Any given place is normally passed over by a polar-orbiting satellite:

options.text: About once a week, on the same day
About every 4 minutes, as with Meteosat
About twice a day, once in each direction
Continuously, throughout the day and night

explanation: A point typically receives a morning pass in one direction and an afternoon or evening pass in the other. Overlap between passes is greatest near the poles.

question: The main disadvantage of polar-orbiting satellites is that they:

options.text: Cannot see the polar regions
Do not provide a continuous view of any one area
Only work at night
Have poorer picture definition than geostationary satellites

explanation: Between passes there is no image of a given area, although the detail of each image is good.

question: A visible satellite image:

options.text: Shows wind speed at the tropopause
Shows reflected sunlight, so it is not available at night
Shows the temperature of cloud tops, both day and night
Shows rainfall intensity directly

explanation: Visible images are easy to interpret, with cloud white, land grey and sea black, but need daylight.

question: On a visible satellite image, the sea normally appears:

options.text: Bright white
Red
Black or very dark
Light grey, the same as cloud

explanation: Water absorbs most visible light, so cloud-free ocean appears dark. Clouds appear white and land grey.

question: An infrared satellite image:

options.text: Is available only in daylight, like a visible image
Shows only land features, not cloud or sea
Shows only reflected sunlight, so it is completely blank at night
Shows the temperature of the radiating surface, day and night

explanation: Infrared sensors measure emitted radiation, so images look much the same by day and by night.

question: On an infrared image, high cloud appears:

options.text: White, because its tops are very cold
Dark grey, because it is thin
Black, because its tops are very cold
Invisible

explanation: The colder the surface, the brighter it is shown. High, cold tops are white; low, warmer cloud is greyer; warm ground is dark.

question: Fog or very low stratus may be difficult to identify on an infrared image because:

options.text: It reflects all the infrared radiation back to space
Its top is at much the same temperature as the surface around it
It is always too cold to be detected by the sensor
Fog only forms at night, when infrared images are not taken

explanation: Low cloud and the sea or ground near it radiate at similar temperatures. A visible image shows fog much more clearly by day.

question: A large area appearing bright white on both visible and infrared images is most likely:

options.text: Warm desert under clear skies
Low stratus or fog over the sea
Clear sea, far from any land or any cloud
Thick, high-topped cloud such as cumulonimbus

explanation: It reflects strongly (thick cloud) and is very cold (high tops). Low cloud is bright on visible but grey on infrared.

question: An area that appears bright on a visible image but dark grey on an infrared image is most likely:

options.text: Clear sea at night
Cumulonimbus with a high anvil
Low cloud or fog with warm tops
High cirrus

explanation: Thick low cloud reflects sunlight well but radiates at nearly surface temperature.

question: Thin cirrus may show up better on infrared than on visible images because:

options.text: It is very cold, even though it reflects little sunlight
It only exists at night, when visible images are blank
It is very warm, so it radiates strongly in the infrared
It reflects more sunlight than thick cloud does

explanation: Thin cirrus can be almost transparent in visible light, but its low temperature makes it stand out on infrared.

question: False-colour images are produced by:

options.text: Painting the cloud features onto the images by hand
Using special colour cameras carried on the polar orbiters
Combining visible images with ground radar data
Converting grey shades, mostly from infrared, into colours

explanation: Colour bands make temperature differences, and so cloud-top heights, easier to see.

question: Because oceans and thick cloud show few features, satellite images are usually presented with:

options.text: A computer-drawn latitude–longitude grid and enhanced coastlines
No geographical reference at all, so as to keep the whole image clear
The positions of radio beacons only
The names of the main airports only

explanation: The grid allows features in the image to be located accurately.

question: Satellite images are most useful to a pilot when:

options.text: Viewed only at night, when infrared is available
Used instead of all other forecasts, as they are always up to date
Used with synoptic charts, and in time-lapse to confirm the forecast
Used only for tracking tropical revolving storms

explanation: Images show what the cloud is actually doing, which helps confirm or question the forecast before departure.

question: Which weather feature is particularly easy to recognise on satellite images?

options.text: Low-level windshear on the approach
A tropical revolving storm, with its spiral bands and eye
Clear air turbulence near the jet stream
Radiation fog lying beneath a thin, broken layer of cirrus

explanation: The organised spiral structure of a tropical revolving storm makes it unmistakable. Clear air turbulence and windshear cannot be seen.

question: Can a standard satellite image show clear air turbulence directly?

options.text: Yes, it shows CAT as black areas on infrared images
No; it can only suggest risk areas, for example from jet-stream cirrus
Yes, but only on images taken at night
Yes, it shows clear air turbulence as red areas on visible images

explanation: Turbulence in clear air is invisible to satellite sensors; only associated cloud features such as jet-stream cirrus or wave clouds give clues.

question: Lines of cloud parallel to a mountain range, downwind of it, on a satellite image suggest:

options.text: A warm front
A sea breeze
Lee waves
Radiation fog

explanation: Standing waves produce bands of cloud on their crests, which show up as regularly spaced lines.

question: The cloud of a frontal system on a satellite image usually appears as:

options.text: Nothing, because fronts cannot be seen from space
A perfect circle centred on the warm sector
Isolated small dots of fair-weather cumulus, with no organised pattern
A long band, often curving into a spiral round the depression centre

explanation: Frontal cloud bands and the comma or spiral shape of a mature depression are clear on both visible and infrared images.

question: Open cells of cumulus on a satellite image over the sea behind a cold front indicate:

options.text: Cold, unstable air being heated from below
Warm, stable air with widespread fog
A warm front approaching
A subsidence inversion with stratus

explanation: Showery convection in polar air over a warmer sea produces a honeycomb pattern of cloud cells.

question: A satellite image shows a large comma-shaped cloud mass over the Atlantic. This usually indicates:

options.text: A developing or mature depression with its frontal cloud band
A sea breeze front along a coastline
An area of radiation fog over the sea
A slow-moving anticyclone with clear skies at its centre

explanation: The comma shape is the frontal band wrapping around the depression centre.

question: Water vapour satellite images show:

options.text: The rate of rainfall reaching the surface at each point
The temperature of the surface of the land and the sea, and nothing else at all, by day and night
The height of the cloud base above the ground at each point
Moisture in the middle and upper troposphere, revealing upper flow even in clear air

explanation: Water vapour channels highlight moist and dry regions aloft and help identify jet streams and upper troughs.

question: Satellite images are particularly valuable over the oceans because:

options.text: Pilots never report weather over oceans
The ocean surface is always clear of cloud
There are very few other observations there
Radar covers the oceans completely

explanation: Satellites fill large gaps between land stations and ships.
